EigenEngine

An integrated research environment for people and AI agents.

A manuscript, its calculations and the evidence for its claims stay connected as the work changes. Beneath the writing interface, a network of state machines records those connections. A diffusion-based memory finds the material a question needs.

The architecture

A calculation changes.
Which claims need another look?

A paragraph can survive a dozen revisions while the calculation behind it has moved on. An agent handed a folder of drafts has to reconstruct that history. A researcher needs to know exactly which version a sentence used.

A claim lives in a container called a conceptric. From the outside, an agent can read its summary, see what it depends on and find the tools it may use. Those tools are verbs. Some open a source. Others change the object and record a new version. Each conceptric is a state machine in the wider network. Opening a chapter returns objects an agent can open in turn, down to the passage or figure it needs.

One claim, several relationships

The claim about equal cost per round belongs to a section, requires an assumption about how a division is priced, and is illustrated by Figure 3. Opening the section, then the claim, then its grounds uses the same operation at successively finer scales.

Changing a recorded input leaves a trail to the work that consumed it. Looking up the pricing rule brings back the relevant passage and figure. The researcher decides how the manuscript should change.

How a preference carries forward

The guessing-machine request guided this revision in conversation. For longer-lived preferences, the author can give feedback the status of a project or passage instruction. Later turns receive the current version where it applies. An authorised update can also revise a shared writing profile, recording the examples behind the change and its previous version.

What the numbers count

A failed attempt has its own receipt. Reading a proposal, producing a new version and accepting an edit are separate events. The count covers these Writing App sessions. Research paper · November 2026

The Cost of Complexity

A Physical Theory of Representation

Gerard McCaul · EigenEngine · 21 pages

Read the paper PDF Related talk ↗

The geometry of refinement

Four times the cells. What does the next division cost?

Each round divides every square into four. If a division costs its area, there are four times as many divisions to pay for, each a quarter of the price. Every round adds the same amount. That gives a logarithmic budget for the number of cells.

Now price each division by wall length. Each cut is half as long, so four times as many cuts double the cost of the next round. The curve visits exactly the same cells.

Figure 3 in the paper ↗
Rounds of division

Left: the register after each round. The blue path visits every cell once, in rank order, and completes each quarter before entering the next, so every sub-square holds a run of consecutive ranks. Gold lines are the divisions, fainter at each round. Right: the total spent on dividing, in units of the first round, for three ways of pricing one division.

Eigen assisted with derivations, figures and drafting using ChatGPT and Claude. Gerard McCaul developed the ideas and takes responsibility for their interpretation and correctness.

The derivations and further results

The paper asks what it costs to organise a physical register when the selector that chooses among registers must also be represented. With additive positional composition, available registers can be reused as digits. The paper derives a logarithmic upper bound on the cheapest budget. A positive limiting price per nat makes that growth logarithmic.

Organisation has a cost of its own

Sixteen symbols are numbered by rank, from the most used to the least used. They can sit in one register of sixteen states or be split across smaller registers. Splitting makes the choice inside each register smaller and adds a second choice: which register. The selector that makes this second choice is a register too, so it has to be paid for.

K(x) = C(Rx) + K(x | Rx)

The cost of reaching a symbol x is the cost of providing and selecting its register Rx, plus the cost of picking x out inside that register.

Arrange as

The blue path joins the symbols in rank order. Gold outlines are registers. Click any symbol to see its address. The symbols and what they stand for are the same in every arrangement. The figure shows how the choice divides. What each part costs is the subject of the register budget.

Erasing a wrong guess releases heat

The paper applies the theory to a deliberately simple model of a computer. It guesses an answer, tests it, and erases the guess if the test fails. Erasing is the step with an unavoidable physical price.

Landauer's principle, an established result in the physics of computing, says the heat Q released by an erasure is at least kBT for each nat of uncertainty removed. That uncertainty is the entropy H of the guesses being erased. kB is Boltzmann's constant and T is the temperature of the surroundings. The paper adds a second floor that needs only the order of the guesses:

⟨Q⟩ ≥ kBT · H ≥ kBT · ⟨log r⟩

Angle brackets mean an average. r is the rank of an erased guess when guesses are listed from most to least probable. The floor depends on how the guesses rank and on nothing about how they are written down: a guess stored as a long number costs no more to erase than one stored as a short number.

A logarithmic price gives a power law in rank

Take the cost of reaching the symbol of rank r to be log r, the form obtained under homogeneous refinement. Suppose the only other thing known about a system is its average cost. Maximum entropy is the standard rule for this situation: among all distributions with that average, take the one that is otherwise as spread out as possible. It is a power law:

p(r) ∝ r−λ

The multiplier λ sets how strongly expensive symbols are avoided. At λ = 1 this is Zipf's law, the pattern that word frequencies follow in many languages. Power laws of this kind have been derived before from other starting points. This derivation needs only the logarithmic cost and the average, and it leaves one free number, λ.

–average cost ⟨log r⟩
–entropy H removed by one erasure
–least heat per erasure at 300 K

Left: the derived family for a vocabulary of 500 symbols; move the slider to change λ. If a memory holding one such symbol is erased, the heat bound gives the third number; a zeptojoule (zJ) is 10−21 joules. Right: a measurement. Blue is word frequency against rank in six public-domain English novels, 1,882,701 words in all. Gold is the member of the family that best fits every word (marked MLE), λ = 1.045. Green is a straight-line fit to ranks 10 to 1,000 only (marked LS), which gives 1.09.

Companion draft · Physical origins of the Kalmár constant
Companion draft

Physical origins of the Kalmár constant

Draft of 19 November 2026 · 8 pages · not yet reviewed

After the paper above was finished, it was given to Eigen with a prompt to apply it. The paper compares ways of organising a register and never charges for choosing among them. Eigen priced that choice in a single pass, running a Claude model. The derivations, numerical checks, figures and text of this draft all came from that pass.

Read the draft (PDF)

Number theory already counts the ways to organise a register

Sixteen ranked symbols can be arranged in registers in eight ways, one for each way of writing 16 as an ordered product of whole numbers. For N symbols the count is the number of ordered factorisations of N. László Kalmár showed in 1931 that its growth is governed by a constant ρ = 1.7286…, the value of s at which the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) = 1 + 1/2s + 1/3s + … equals 2.

The draft reads Kalmár's constant as a capacity

If registers cost nothing to exist, each extra nat of budget multiplies the number of symbols a register can hold by e, and the number of ways to organise them by eρ. Give every register the existence cost K0 of the register budget and the exponent falls below ρ, along the curve shown. It approaches 1, the value of λ at which the Zipf family of the rank distribution can no longer be normalised for an unlimited vocabulary. The limit on how often symbols can be used in the first paper is therefore also the limit on how many ways expensive registers can be organised.

4 → 10binary digits

The draft also prices a register that stores the choice of its own organisation, then the organisation of that record, until nothing is left unrecorded. A binary register of k digits needs k(k + 1)/2 digits to do this. For sixteen symbols that is ten binary digits; four are enough for the symbols alone.

The number theory in the draft is classical. Its reading of ρ as a capacity, the curve above and the results on registers that record their own organisation are stated as new: the draft reports that a literature search did not find them and that the search was not exhaustive. It also predicts how self-organising hierarchies should branch, and says this prediction has not been tested against data. Its results are for registers whose sub-registers all have the same size, and they give the cost of holding an organisation, with nothing yet on the cost of changing it. The record does not always close: of the registers holding 2 to 10,000 symbols, the draft finds 817 that never finish recording themselves.

The draft's acknowledgements record who did what. They name Claude, the model Eigen was running. The results on capacity, on the ensemble of organisations and on self-recording registers were derived by the model at the author's prompting. The final hierarchy was proposed by the author and formalised by the model. The question the draft answers is one the first paper leaves open, and Eigen answered it in one pass.
